summary: Describes using pre-shared keys in the Cryptographic Message Syntax so that protected messages stay safe even if a large quantum computer later breaks today's key transport and key agreement. It addresses the risk of stored traffic being decrypted in the future.

plainLanguage.summary: If two friends already share a secret word, they can use it to lock messages. Even a future super-computer could not easily break that.

questions: how to make cms quantum resistant
subtitle: Mixing a pre-shared key into CMS key management so that stored messages stay safe from a future quantum computer.

tldr.problem: CMS key transport and key agreement (RSA, Diffie-Hellman, ECDH) could be broken by a large-scale quantum computer, so someone who stores CMS-protected traffic today could decrypt it later.
tldr.mechanism: Two new recipient-info types, keyTransPSK and keyAgreePSK, run the normal public-key step and then mix its output with a pre-shared key in a key derivation function to produce the key-encryption key that wraps the content key.
tldr.outcome: If the PSK has enough entropy and the KDF and ciphers are quantum resistant, today's CMS messages can resist a future quantum attacker. It is a Proposed Standard.

facts.label: Minimum KEK and content key length

today: RFC 8696 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2019. It has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: The Quantum Problem for CMS
sections.content:
The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) supports key transport and key agreement algorithms such as RSA, Diffie-Hellman and Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman. A large-scale quantum computer could break these. The RFC notes it is an open question whether such a computer can be built and when, but an adversary who stores CMS-protected communications today could decrypt them if one appears.

Once quantum-secure key management algorithms exist, CMS will be extended to support them if the syntax needs it. In the near term, this document mixes the output of existing key transport and key agreement with a pre-shared key (PSK). The RFC also says a strong PSK guards against a cryptanalytic breakthrough on classic public key algorithms and against concerns about undisclosed trapdoors in Diffie-Hellman parameters.

CMS key management based on symmetric key-encryption keys and on passwords is not covered, because it is already quantum resistant when used with adequate key sizes.
sections.plainLanguage: Today's locks might someday be picked by a machine that does not exist yet. Adding a secret both friends already know makes the lock much harder, even for that machine.

sections.title: How the PSK Is Mixed In
sections.content:
In both techniques the sender randomly generates the content-encryption key (CEK) and encrypts it with a symmetric key-encryption key (KEK) that depends on the PSK. The PSK MUST be distributed to the sender and all recipients out of band, by a means that is not vulnerable to a future quantum computer, and an identifier MUST be assigned to it. A PSK is expected to be used with many messages, with a lifetime of weeks or months.

With key transport, the sender also generates a random key-derivation key (KDK), encrypts it to each recipient's public key, and uses the KDF to mix the PSK and the KDK into the KEK, which encrypts the CEK. With key agreement, the sender and recipient establish a pairwise KEK1 from their key pair, the KDF mixes it with the PSK to give KEK2, and KEK2 encrypts the CEK.

Both techniques ride in the OtherRecipientInfo type of RFC 5652, each identified by its own object identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: First the friends use the normal lock to share a small key. Then they stir that key together with their secret word to make the real key that locks the message.

sections.title: keyTransPSK
sections.content:
Per-recipient information is a KeyTransPSKRecipientInfo, indicated by id-ori-keyTransPSK. Its fields are version (MUST be 0), pskid (an OCTET STRING identifying the PSK, not necessarily human readable), kdfAlgorithm, keyEncryptionAlgorithm, ktris and encryptedKey.

The ktris field holds one KeyTransRecipientInfo per recipient, but its encryptedKey carries the key-derivation key instead of the content key. The outer encryptedKey is the CEK encrypted with the KEK that the KDF produced. One instance serves one or more recipients that share the same PSK.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender hides a small key in each friend's personal lockbox, then mixes it with the shared secret to make the key that locks the message key.

sections.title: keyAgreePSK
sections.content:
Per-recipient information is a KeyAgreePSKRecipientInfo, indicated by id-ori-keyAgreePSK. It has version (MUST be 0), pskid, originator, an optional ukm, kdfAlgorithm, keyEncryptionAlgorithm and recipientEncryptedKeys.

Implementations MUST support all three alternatives for specifying the sender's public key in originator. The optional User Keying Material (ukm) makes each pairwise key different; implementations MUST accept a structure that includes it, and those that do not use UKMs MUST handle its presence gracefully. The KDF mixes the PSK with the pairwise KEK to produce a second KEK of the same length, and that second KEK encrypts the CEK.
sections.plainLanguage: Here the two friends first agree on a shared key by swapping public pieces. Then they stir in their secret word to make a stronger key.

sections.title: Key Derivation Inputs
sections.content:
The RFC uses the vocabulary of HKDF from RFC 5869. The inputs are IKM (the key-derivation key for keyTransPSK, the pairwise key-encryption key for keyAgreePSK), an optional salt, the output length L in octets, and info. The output OKM is exactly L octets and is the key-encryption key.

The info value is the DER encoding of CMSORIforPSKOtherInfo, which includes the PSK itself, a keyMgmtAlgType (5 for key transport, 10 for key agreement), the key-encryption algorithm identifier, pskLength and kdkLength. An acceptable KDF MUST accept IKM, L and info, MAY accept salt and other inputs, and all inputs MUST influence the output. Any salt or other inputs MUST be given as parameters of the KeyDerivationAlgorithmIdentifier.
sections.plainLanguage: The recipe takes the shared small key, the secret word and a note saying which method was used. It blends them into a key of exactly the right size.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A large-scale quantum computer essentially negates the key transport or key agreement step, so an attacker could discover the key-derivation key, and it effectively halves the strength of a symmetric algorithm. Therefore the PSK needs at least 256 bits of entropy to provide 128 bits of security, the KDF needs to be quantum resistant and produce a KEK of at least 256 bits, and the content-encryption key also needs to be at least 256 bits.

The effective security is that of the weakest link: 256-bit AES content wrapped with a 128-bit AES key gives at most 128 bits. Compromise of the PSK makes content vulnerable to a future quantum computer. Implementers should not protect the same content with both a traditional and a PSK variant, nor send the same content in two messages, one of each kind, because that could let an eavesdropper correlate them.

The PSK need not be known only to the sender and recipients, but if a group shares it, members can record each other's traffic and decrypt it later, and there are more chances for the PSK to be stolen. Keys must be randomly generated. A ProVerif proof cited in the RFC indicates that an attacker able to break Diffie-Hellman cannot disrupt delivery of the CEK or learn it from the exchange.
sections.plainLanguage: The secret word has to be long and truly random, and kept private. If it leaks, the extra protection is gone.

sections.title: IANA and Privacy
sections.content:
IANA assigned an object identifier for the ASN.1 module and one new entry, id-ori (arc 13 under S/MIME). It also created a registry for Other Recipient Info identifiers with the Specification Required policy, and recorded id-ori-keyTransPSK as 1 and id-ori-keyAgreePSK as 2 in it.

On privacy, an observer can see which parties use each PSK by watching the PSK identifiers. The RFC argues this barely weakens privacy, because recipients are already identified in the key transport and key agreement structures.
sections.plainLanguage: The new key types got official numbers in a public list. Someone watching can see which secret word is used, but they could already tell who the message was for.
